question.text: Which investment-related risk is borne by the individual in a Defined Contribution (DC) pension plan but is generally borne by the employer/sponsor in a Defined Benefit (DB) plan?

answer.text: Inflation risk on post-retirement household expenses
Investment risk on the accumulated retirement corpus (returns falling below expectations)
Cost of providing for an unmarried adult child after the subscriber's death

explanation.text: The Logic: The stem asks specifically for an investment-related risk allocated differently between DB and DC. In a DC plan, the individual bears the investment risk on the corpus - poor market returns translate directly into a smaller retirement pot. In a DB plan, the employer/sponsor promises a defined benefit and therefore bears the investment risk on the underlying assets (NISM Series XVII, June 2025, pp.15-16). The Trap: Inflation risk and health-expense risk are borne by retirees under BOTH DB and DC arrangements, so they are not differentiators. The audit flagged the original because the "risk of increasing life expectancy" (longevity risk) option was also defensibly valid - p.18 states that an individual in a DC plan assumes both investment risk and longevity risk, while DB plans protected the subscriber from longevity risk. That made two options correct under the original stem. Note: The original was ambiguous because the longevity-risk option was also a DC-only risk per p.18. The stem has been narrowed to "investment-related risk" specifically, and the longevity option has been replaced with a household-expense item that applies to both DB and DC, leaving "investment risk on the accumulated corpus" as the unique answer.
